plan: Ten new SAT R&W items aimed at upper difficulty: noncommittal (WIC), Roman harbor concrete purpose, crow social-learning evidence, trail-survey sampling inference, four-day-week selection cross-text, percent-versus-count survey data, either/or agreement, dangling introductory modifier, specification transition, Amazon/Congo similarity synthesis. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A careful report
passages.text: The review committee's report on the proposed stadium was notably ______: it listed the plan's costs and benefits in detail but declined to say whether the city should go ahead with the project.

passages.title: Roman harbor concrete
passages.text: Some concrete structures built in Roman harbors have survived roughly two thousand years of exposure to seawater, while modern concrete in similar conditions can crumble within decades. The difference long puzzled engineers. Analyzing samples from Roman harbors, researchers found that seawater seeping through the concrete reacted with volcanic ash in the original mix, growing new mineral crystals that filled cracks and strengthened the material over time.

passages.title: Crows and masks
passages.text: In a long-term study, researchers wearing a distinctive mask briefly captured and released several wild crows on a college campus. For years afterward, crows on the campus scolded and dived at anyone wearing that mask but ignored people wearing a different, neutral mask. The researchers hypothesized that crows learn to recognize dangerous people not only from their own experience but also by observing other crows.

passages.title: Birds along trails
passages.text: An ecologist surveyed bird species in a forest by having observers walk the forest's trails at dawn and record every species they heard singing. Observers recorded more species near trailheads than deep in the forest. However, because the observers walked only along trails and could hear birds only within about fifty meters, the ecologist cautioned that ______

passages.title: A shorter week
passages.text:
Text 1
An economist studying companies that adopted a four-day workweek found that their output per employee rose by an average of 8 percent in the following year. She argues that a shorter week could raise productivity across the economy.

Text 2
A labor researcher notes that the companies in the study chose to try the four-day week, and many were firms whose managers already believed their work could be done in less time. Results from such firms, he argues, may say little about how a shorter week would work at companies that would not have chosen it.

passages.title: Rural and urban survey
passages.text: In a state survey, 200 rural residents and 800 urban residents were asked whether they had used a public library in the past month. Of the rural residents, 30 percent said yes; of the urban residents, 20 percent said yes. A reporter claims that more urban residents than rural residents in the survey had used a library, even though a smaller percentage of urban residents had.

passages.title: Conference plans
passages.text: Either the study's lead author or her two coauthors ______ expected to present the team's findings at next month's conference on coastal erosion.

passages.title: Two writers
passages.text: Having spent a decade comparing the handwriting, ink, and paper of the letters, ______ that they were written by two different people rather than one.

passages.title: Load ratings
passages.text: The new bridge across the river was designed to carry far heavier traffic than the one it replaced. ______ engineers rated it to support trucks weighing up to forty tons, about twice the limit on the old bridge.

passages.title: Two great rivers
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Amazon River carries more water to the sea than any other river.
- The Congo River carries the second-largest volume of water.
- Both rivers drain large tropical rainforests.
- The Amazon is roughly 6,400 kilometers long; the Congo is roughly 4,700 kilometers long.
- Parts of the Congo are more than 200 meters deep.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: declined to say whether the city should go ahead
candidates.explanation: A report that lays out costs and benefits but refuses to recommend a course is "noncommittal."

A.rationale: A partisan report would take a side, but this one declines to recommend anything.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the report repeated itself or duplicated another report.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the report was meant to provoke anger; it simply avoided a recommendation.

hints: What did the report decline to do?
candidates.remember: Use the explanation after the colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain how a puzzle about an ancient material's durability was solved
choices.B: To argue that builders today should stop using modern concrete in harbors
choices.C: To compare the harbors built by Romans with those built by later empires
choices.D: To describe the methods Romans used to mine volcanic ash for construction

candidates.explanation: The text presents a puzzle (why Roman harbor concrete lasted so long) and then reports the finding that explains it.

B.rationale: The text explains a finding; it makes no recommendation about modern building.

C.rationale: No later empires or their harbors are discussed.

D.rationale: The text mentions ash in the mix but not how it was obtained.

hints: What problem does the text raise, and what does the rest of it do?
candidates.remember: Purpose answers describe what the whole text does.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (supporting a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.A: Crows that had been captured scolded people wearing the captors' mask more often than any other crows did.
choices.B: Crows on the campus scolded people wearing the captors' mask whether or not those people came near them.
choices.C: Crows on the campus ignored people wearing the neutral mask even when those people carried food.
choices.D: Crows hatched after the captures, never captured themselves, also scolded people wearing the captors' mask.

candidates.evidence: but also by observing other crows
candidates.explanation: Crows that were never captured can only have learned to fear the mask from other crows, which is exactly the social learning the hypothesis proposes.

A.rationale: This reflects the crows' own experience and says nothing about learning from other crows.

B.rationale: This concerns how the crows react, not how they learned to react.

C.rationale: This shows the crows discriminate between masks but not that they learned from other crows.

hints: Which part of the hypothesis goes beyond a crow's own experience?

strategy.explanation: Find a group of crows that could not have learned on their own.

candidates.remember: Support for a hypothesis must test the part that is new or disputed.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: birds in the forest probably prefer to live near trailheads rather than in the interior.
choices.B: the survey may not show how the number of species changes away from the trails.
choices.C: dawn is the only time of day when singing birds can be reliably counted.
choices.D: trails reduce the number of bird species living in nearby parts of the forest.

candidates.evidence: could hear birds only within about fifty meters
candidates.explanation: Observers sampled only a narrow band along the trails, so the survey cannot speak to areas away from them; the caution is about what the data can show.

A.rationale: This is the conclusion the ecologist is cautioning against drawing from the survey.

C.rationale: The caution concerns where observers could detect birds, not when.

D.rationale: This contradicts the finding of more species near trailheads and is not what the caution is about.

hints: What part of the forest did the observers never sample?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the method could and could not detect.

candidates.remember: A sample can only describe the places and conditions it covered.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the labor researcher (Text 2) most likely respond to the economist's argument in Text 1?

choices.A: He would agree that the firms' gains show that all companies should adopt a four-day week soon.
choices.B: He would argue that productivity at the firms studied actually fell after the four-day week began.
choices.C: He would say the firms studied may not be typical, so their gains may not apply elsewhere.
choices.D: He would argue that most workers would rather keep a five-day week than switch to a shorter one.

candidates.evidence: companies that would not have chosen it
candidates.explanation: Text 2 accepts the results but points out that the firms chose the policy and expected it to work, so generalizing to all firms is unwarranted.

A.rationale: He questions whether the results apply to other companies, so he would not agree.

B.rationale: He does not dispute the reported gain, only what it implies for other firms.

D.rationale: Worker preferences are never discussed in Text 2.

hints: Does the researcher dispute the data or how far it can be applied?

strategy.explanation: Separate what he accepts from what he questions.

candidates.remember: A self-selected sample may not represent the whole population.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the survey to support the reporter's claim?

choices.A: 160 urban residents said yes versus 60 rural residents, though 20 percent is below 30 percent.
choices.B: 30 percent of rural residents said yes, compared with only 20 percent of urban residents.
choices.C: The survey included 800 urban residents but only 200 rural residents, four times as many people.
choices.D: Fewer than one-third of the residents in each group said they had used a public library.

candidates.evidence: more urban residents than rural residents in the survey had used a library
candidates.explanation: 20 percent of 800 is 160 and 30 percent of 200 is 60, so more urban residents said yes even though their percentage was lower. Only A gives both parts.

B.rationale: This supports only the second half of the claim and says nothing about the numbers of people.

C.rationale: Group sizes alone do not show how many in each group said yes.

D.rationale: This is true of both groups but does not compare them as the claim does.

hints: What would you need to compute to compare numbers of people?

strategy.explanation: Convert each percentage to a count.

candidates.remember: A smaller percentage of a larger group can still be a larger number.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: When subjects are joined by "either ... or," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. "Coauthors" is plural, so "are" is correct.

A.rationale: With "either ... or," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "coauthors," which is plural.

C.rationale: "Was" is singular and also shifts to the past, but the event is still to come.

D.rationale: "Has been" is singular and does not agree with the nearer subject, "coauthors."

hints: Which subject is closer to the verb?

strategy.explanation: Find the subject nearest the blank.

candidates.remember: With either/or and neither/nor, match the verb to the nearer subject.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.B: it was concluded by the historian
choices.C: the conclusion the historian reached was

candidates.explanation: The introductory phrase describes whoever spent a decade comparing the letters, so "the historian" must come right after the comma.

A.rationale: The phrase "Having spent a decade" must describe a person, but here it would describe a conclusion.

B.rationale: "It" did not spend a decade comparing the letters.

C.rationale: A conclusion cannot spend a decade comparing letters.

hints: Who spent a decade comparing the letters?

strategy.explanation: Put that person right after the comma.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier describes the noun right after it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: trucks weighing up to forty tons
candidates.explanation: The second sentence gives exact figures for the general claim in the first, so "Specifically" fits.

A.rationale: Nothing in the second sentence goes against the first.

B.rationale: The second sentence does not replace the first; it gives details of it.

D.rationale: The second sentence does not describe a similar but separate case.

hints: Does the second sentence contrast, add a new case, or give details?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Use "specifically" when a sentence gives precise details of a general claim.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two rivers. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: At roughly 6,400 kilometers, the Amazon is about 1,700 kilometers longer than the 4,700-kilometer Congo.
choices.B: Parts of the Congo River are more than 200 meters deep, making it unusually deep for a river.
choices.C: The Amazon River carries more water to the sea than any other river anywhere on Earth, including the Congo.
choices.D: Both the Amazon and the Congo drain vast tropical rainforests and carry more water than any other rivers.

candidates.evidence: Both rivers drain large tropical rainforests.
candidates.explanation: Only D describes features the two rivers share: both drain rainforests and both are at the top in volume.

A.rationale: This emphasizes a difference in length, not a similarity.

hints: Which choice mentions both rivers and something they have in common?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: For a similarity goal, the answer must describe both items and what they share.
